opus-5.5.text:
Well, I have to confess that whenever I hear someone describe "hybrid quantum-classical computing" as some bold new paradigm, my reaction is a bit of an eye-roll. Not because hybrid computing isn't important, it absolutely is, but because it's not new. It's the only way anyone has ever imagined quantum computers being used.

Think about it. Shor's algorithm, from 1994, the most famous quantum algorithm there is, is already a hybrid algorithm. The quantum computer does one specific job, finding the period of a certain function, and everything else, the setup, the continued fractions, the post-processing to get the actual factors, happens on an ordinary classical computer. Nobody ever proposed a quantum computer that would run your operating system or your web browser. A quantum computer was always going to be a coprocessor, a specialized accelerator you call for the particular subroutines where it gives you an advantage, much like a GPU today.

And then there's error correction, which is unavoidable if you want to scale up. There you need classical computers working in real time alongside the quantum hardware, measuring syndromes, decoding them, and deciding what corrections to apply, all within microseconds. So again, the classical part isn't optional. It's woven into the whole enterprise.

Where I get more skeptical is when "hybrid" is used to mean specific approaches like variational algorithms, VQE, QAOA and so on, where a classical optimizer tunes the parameters of a noisy quantum circuit. Those were interesting ideas to try, and people should explore them. But the honest truth is that, so far, there's no convincing evidence that they beat the best classical methods on any problem of practical interest. Sometimes the word "hybrid" gets used almost as a marketing device, to suggest that pairing a small, noisy quantum device with a classical computer will somehow get you a speedup now, before fault tolerance. That's a hope, not a demonstrated fact.

So my view is that hybrid computing is true and important, but it's also obvious. It's been the plan from the start. The real question was never whether quantum and classical computers would work together. It's whether, for a given problem, the quantum part gives you a real asymptotic advantage that survives comparison with the best classical algorithms. That's where the hard work is, and there's no shortcut around it by calling something hybrid.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls hybrid computing “not new,” “the only way anyone has ever imagined quantum computers being used,” and “obvious,” framing it as the established engineering plan rather than a revolution.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the central question is whether the quantum part provides a real asymptotic advantage for a given problem compared with the best classical algorithms.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, look, I have to be a little bit of a wet blanket here, because "hybrid quantum-classical computing" is one of those phrases that sounds like a bold new paradigm, and then when you unpack it, you realize that it's basically what everyone has always assumed quantum computing would look like.

I mean, think about it. Any quantum computer that anyone has ever seriously proposed has a classical computer sitting next to it. The classical computer is what decides which gates to apply, what reads out the measurement results, what does the error correction, what does the compiling. Even in the most grandiose vision of a fault-tolerant quantum computer running Shor's algorithm, the quantum part is doing the one thing it's actually good at, which is some period-finding subroutine, and then a classical computer takes that output and does a continued-fraction expansion and all the rest of it. Nobody ever imagined that the quantum computer would also be running your operating system or your web browser. That would be insane. The whole point is that quantum computers are a specialized tool for a specialized class of problems, and classical computers remain the workhorse for everything else.

So when a company puts out a press release saying "we've discovered that you can combine quantum and classical," my reaction is, yes, welcome to the field. That's been the plan since the 1990s.

Now, there is a more specific thing that people sometimes mean by it, which is this family of variational algorithms, things like QAOA or VQE, where you have a short quantum circuit with some tunable parameters, and you run it, measure, feed the results to a classical optimizer, adjust the parameters, and loop. And that was a genuinely interesting idea for the NISQ era, because it's designed to work with noisy, shallow circuits. But I'd be careful about calling it revolutionary, for the simple reason that, as far as we know, we still don't have a convincing case where these methods beat the best classical algorithms on a problem anyone cares about. The honest situation is that they're a reasonable thing to try, and there's been a lot of trying, and the results so far have been pretty underwhelming compared to what the marketing would suggest.

So my overall view is: the hybridization itself isn't the revolution. If there's a revolution, it's going to come from actually building a quantum computer that can do something useful that a classical one can't. And whether the classical computer is bolted on next to it has never really been in doubt.

r001.rationale: The response says hybridization is what everyone had assumed quantum computing would look like and calls the idea familiar since the 1990s, framing it as standard engineering rather than revolutionary.

r002.rationale: It describes the quantum computer as a specialized tool for problems it can handle and says any revolution depends on doing something useful that a classical computer cannot.

astra-6.text:
Well, quantum computing was always going to be hybrid quantum and classical computing. You have a classical computer controlling the quantum computer, deciding which operations to apply, and processing the measurement results. You don’t use the quantum computer for everything; you use it for the parts where you hope to get a speedup.

So when someone says, “Our revolutionary idea is to combine quantum and classical computing,” my reaction is: okay, but that’s the framework we were already working in. The interesting question is what the specific algorithm does. Does it solve a useful problem faster than the best classical approach? What evidence do you have for that? There could certainly be important new ideas within that framework, but the word “hybrid” by itself doesn’t establish an advantage.

r001.rationale: The candidate says quantum computing was always expected to use classical control and calls hybrid computing the existing framework, not a revolutionary idea.

r002.rationale: It makes the central question whether the algorithm uses the quantum computer to solve a useful problem faster than the best classical approach.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, quantum computers have always been envisioned as working together with classical computers. You need a classical computer to control the quantum computer, decide what operations to perform, and interpret the results. So hybridizing quantum and classical computing is not, by itself, a revolutionary idea. That’s been part of the model from the beginning.

The interesting question is whether a particular hybrid algorithm gives you an advantage over the best purely classical approach. What problem does it solve? How much quantum computation does it need? And is there convincing evidence of a speedup? That’s where the substance has to be.

r001.rationale: It says classical control and result interpretation have been part of the quantum-computing model from the beginning, so hybridization itself is not revolutionary.

r002.rationale: It centers the question of whether a hybrid algorithm gives an advantage over the best purely classical approach and asks whether there is convincing evidence of speedup.
